title: Dec 2015 (Paper III)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (75/75 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Thomas Bowdler, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Thomas and enrietta Bowdler’s edition of The Family Shakespeare ave rise to the word
“Bowdlerize”. What does it mean ?
items.explanation: Thomas Bowdler and his sister Henrietta published The Family Shakespeare (1807), expurgating sexual, vulgar, or irreverent words to make Shakespeare suitable for family reading, giving rise to the verb 'bowdlerize' meaning to censor or expurgate indelicate language.

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
First follow __________ and your judgement frame. By her just __________ , which is still
the same. Supply the appropriate words to fill in the blanks.
items.explanation: In An Essay on Criticism (1711), Alexander Pope establishes the fundamental Neoclassical aesthetic rule: 'First follow Nature, and your judgment frame / By her just standard, which is still the same: / Unerring NATURE, still divinely bright...'

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Michael West
items.stem:
Preparation of vocabulary list for the purpose of English language teaching was carried out
by H__________.
items.explanation: Michael West was a pioneering British ELT educator who developed the famous General Service List (GSL, 1953), selecting and frequency-ranking 2,000 core English word families essential for foreign learners.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Michael Hardt, Antonio Negri
items.stem:
Michael ardt and Antonio Negri prefer to use H“Empire” rather than imperialism.
According to them :
options: There is only one empire and we had better recognize it. ence the Empire with E upper case.
There may be many empires but only one is patently visible and operational. That is denoted by Empire with E upper case.
The present day empire does not have an identifiable location or centre. ence we ought to differentiate this view of Empire with E upper case.
The culturally dominant global empire is the only one that really matters. We signify that Empire with E upper case.
items.explanation: In Empire (2000), Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri conceptualize 'Empire' (capitalized) as a decentred, deterritorialized global apparatus of governance without an imperialist national center or border, distinguishing it from historical European imperialism.

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T. S. Eliot, P. B. Shelley
items.stem: Who among the following critics discerned in the Shelleyan Lyric the signs “of adolescence” ?
items.explanation: In The Use of Poetry and the Use of Criticism (1933), T. S. Eliot criticized P. B. Shelley's poetry and philosophical ideas as immature, remarking that some of Shelley's lyrics and ideas were intensely embarrassing as signs of permanent adolescence.

items.title: Q6 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Cleanth Brooks, John Crowe Ransom
items.stem:
Two among the following critical journals became strongly associated with New Criticism.
(a)
Partisan Review
(b)
Southern Review
(c)
Kenyon Review
(d)
udson Review
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: The Southern Review (founded by Cleanth Brooks and Robert Penn Warren in 1935) and The Kenyon Review (founded by John Crowe Ransom in 1939) served as the primary institutional quarterly journals defining American New Criticism.

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Robert Burton, Richard Hooker, Thomas Browne, Thomas Nashe
items.stem:
Match the columns :
(a)
Robert Burton
(i)
Urn Burial
(b)
Richard ooker
(ii)
The Unfortunate Traveller
(c)
Thomas Browne
(iii)
The Anatomy of Melancholy
(d)
Thomas Nashe
(iv)
Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Politie
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: Robert Burton authored The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) (iii); Richard Hooker wrote Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Politie (1594) (iv); Sir Thomas Browne wrote Hydriotaphia, Urn Burial (1658) (i); and Thomas Nashe authored the picaresque romance The Unfortunate Traveller (1594) (ii).

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · John Webster
items.stem:
Which of the following characters in The White Devil describes the glory of great men as :
“Glories, like glow-worms a far off shine bright / But looked to near have neither heat nor
light”.
items.explanation: In John Webster's Jacobean revenge tragedy The White Devil (1612, Act V scene 1), the Machiavellian malcontent Flamineo cynically reflects on political greatness: 'Glories, like glow-worms, afar off shine bright, / But looked to near, have neither heat nor light.'

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit II: Poetry · Philip Larkin
items.stem:
In which of Philip Larkin’s poem does he refer to “long uneven lines” of men waiting to be
enlisted for the war ?
(“Never such innocence again” concludes the poem)
items.explanation: In 'MCMXIV' (The Whitsun Weddings, 1964), Philip Larkin gazes at archival photographs of August 1914 enlistment volunteers outside cricket grounds ('Those long uneven lines / Standing as patiently...'), concluding memorably 'Never such innocence again.'

items.title: Q10 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Franz Kafka
items.stem:
In Franz Kafka’s Metamorphosis, Gregor Samsa one morning found himself changed in his
bed to a monstrous kind of vermin. The most difficult thing for Samsa was :
options: to look at his image in the mirror
to remember what happened the day before
items.explanation: In Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis (1915), Gregor Samsa's transformation produces an animalistic, unintelligible chirping squeak in his vocal cords, rendering human verbal communication impossible when his family and chief clerk address him.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Ivan Turgenev
items.stem: Identify the individual who is a nihilist from the following :
options: Pechorin in A ero of Our Times
items.explanation: In Ivan Turgenev's novel Fathers and Sons (1862), the medical student Yevgeny Bazarov is the quintessential embodiment of Russian 1860s nihilism, repudiating all traditional authority, faith, family sentiments, and Romantic aesthetics in favor of pure natural science.

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Alexander Pushkin
items.stem:
Which of these works in nineteenth-century Russian fiction originated the type of a
Superfluous Man ?
options: The Diary of a Superfluous Man
A ero of our Own Times
items.explanation: The archetypal 'Superfluous Man' (lishny chelovek)—an intelligent, aristocratic, but alienated and cynical figure paralyzed by ennui—originated with Alexander Pushkin's titular protagonist in his masterpiece verse-novel Eugene Onegin (1833).

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Classical & Ancient Background · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
What is Gilgamesh ?
(a)
a Babylonian epic poem
(b)
a series of nomic verses
(c)
a classical play
(d)
the story of a harsh ruler
items.explanation: The Epic of Gilgamesh is an ancient Mesopotamian/Babylonian epic poem inscribed on cuneiform clay tablets (a) recounting the heroic exploits, grief, quest for immortality, and harsh reign of Gilgamesh, the tyrannical king of Uruk (d).

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Noah Webster
items.stem:
American Dictionary of the English Language was the work of H__________ published in
__________.
items.explanation: Noah Webster published An American Dictionary of the English Language in two quarto volumes in 1828, standardizing distinctive American orthography (such as 'color' for 'colour' and 'center' for 'centre') and documenting American idioms.

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Amitav Ghosh
items.stem:
Which of the following texts of Amitav Ghosh is based on the refugee occupation of an
island in the Sundarvans ?
items.explanation: Amitav Ghosh's novel The Hungry Tide (2004) weaves contemporary ecological and dolphin research in the Sundarbans mangrove archipelago with the historical 1979 Marichjhapi massacre, wherein thousands of Dalit Hindu refugees were forcibly evicted.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem: Which of the following is described by Robert Browning as “A Child’s Story” ?
items.explanation: Robert Browning composed 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin' in 1842 for William Macready's young son Willy, deliberately subtitling the narrative poem 'A Child's Story' when collecting it in Dramatic Lyrics.

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Cleanth Brooks
items.stem:
Identify the New Critic who served as the cultural attaché at the American Embassy in
London from 1964 to 1966 :
items.explanation: Renowned Southern New Critic Cleanth Brooks (co-author of Understanding Poetry and author of The Well Wrought Urn) served with distinction as Cultural Attaché at the United States Embassy in London from 1964 to 1966.

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Mark Twain
items.stem:
“The Gilded Age” refers to a period of American history between 1870 and the first decades
of the twentieth century.
Who among the following American writers is credited with the coining of the term ?
items.explanation: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner coined 'The Gilded Age' as the title of their collaborative 1873 satirical novel, mocking post-Civil War American society as covered with a glittering golden veneer that hid rampant political corruption and greed.

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Edward Gibbon
items.stem:
The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in six volumes was a great achievement by Edward
Gibbon. It was published between 1776 and 1788, two significant dates that.
options: Signalled the end of the Napoleonic wars and the rise of Feudalism.
Signalled the American Revolution and the French Revolution.
Covered the fall of peasantry and the rise of bureaucracy in England.
Suggest the period of Queen Anne’s reign.
items.explanation: Edward Gibbon published the six volumes of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire between 1776 and 1788, dates which bookended two epochal modern revolutions: the 1776 American Declaration of Independence and the threshold of the 1789 French Revolution.

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem:
Being so caught up, so mastered by the brute __________ of the air, Did she put on his
knowledge with his power, Before the __________ beak could let her drop.
Yeats, “Leda and the Swan”.
Choose the right words for the blanks :
items.explanation: In W. B. Yeats's sonnet 'Leda and the Swan' (1923), the octave and sestet pivot on the lines: 'Being so caught up, so mastered by the brute blood of the air, / Did she put on his knowledge with his power / Before the indifferent beak could let her drop?'

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · William Empson, Julia Kristeva, Mikhail Bakhtin
items.stem:
Match the following :
Terms
Description
(a)
Ambiguity
(i)
A term coined by Julia Kristeva to refer to the fact
that texts are constituted by a “tissue of citations”.
(b)
Aporia
(ii)
A term used by Mikhail Bakhtin to describe the
variety of languages and voices within a novel.
(c)
Intertextuality
(iii)
An irresolvable internal contradiction or logical
disjunction in a text, usually associated with
deconstructive thinking.
(d)
eteroglossia
(iv)
A term made famous by William Empson to
indicate that a word, phrase, or text can be
interpreted in more than one way.
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: Ambiguity was defined by William Empson in Seven Types of Ambiguity (iv); Aporia is deconstruction's term for an irresolvable textual contradiction (iii); Intertextuality was coined by Julia Kristeva (i); and Heteroglossia was formulated by Mikhail Bakhtin (ii).

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Mary Shelley, John Milton
items.stem:
Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay
To mould me man ? Did I solicit thee
From darkness to promote me ?
Which nineteenth-century work bears these lines from Paradise Lost as epigraph ?
items.explanation: Mary Shelley chose Adam's despairing reproach from Milton's Paradise Lost (Book X, 743–745: 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man? Did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?') as the epigraph on the title page of Frankenstein (1818).

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
A literary researcher now faced with choosing between a print text and its digital
counterpart chooses the latter mostly to :
options: facilitate the consultation of an exhaustive bibliography
avoid the expense of buying books
look for specific words and phrases and lines
enhance his/her understanding of textual variants, if any, between the two media
items.explanation: In modern literary research, scholars consult digital editions and digitized corpora primarily for computational text-searchability—enabling instantaneous concordance searches for specific terms, recurring collocations, lexical variations, and textual patterns.

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Civil War, Interregnum & Restoration · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Butler
items.stem:
Which of the following statements on udibras are true ?
(a)
It is a novel written by Matthew Prior.
(b)
It is a satirical poem published in 3 parts.
(c)
udibras was written by Samuel Butler.
(d)
udibras discusses complex issues of justice, politics and religion.
items.explanation: Samuel Butler's Hudibras is a brilliant Mock-heroic mock-epic satire written in rhyming octosyllabic 'Hudibrastic' couplets, published in three parts (1663, 1664, 1678) ridiculing Puritan hypocrisy; statements (b) and (c) are true.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · L. C. Knights, A. C. Bradley, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
The formalist critic __________ mocked the character - based criticism of __________ by
posing a famous question, “ow many children had Lady Macbeth” ?
items.explanation: Cambridge critic L. C. Knights published his celebrated Scrutiny essay 'How Many Children Had Lady Macbeth?' in 1933, delivering a witty formalist assault against A. C. Bradley's Victorian tendency to treat Shakespearean dramatic figures as autonomous biographical persons.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following pair of words does not have two different vowel lides ?
items.explanation: A vowel glide is a diphthong where the articulatory organs move from one vocalic position to another. The words 'eight' and 'ate' share the identical closing diphthong /eɪ/, and thus do NOT possess two different vowel glides.

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Assertion (A) :
Arts will often work obliquely, by myth or symbol. They may make their
best ‘criticism of life’ simply by being; they may best state by not stating.
Reason (R) :
It follows, if even only part of all this is true, that the arts do have an
important social function. [...] Arts can ive reater depth to a society’s
sense of itself. [...] A country without great art might be a powerful collection
of thriving earthworms but would be a sorry society.
options: Reason (R) is perfectly aligned with Assertion (A)
items.explanation: In cultural and aesthetic theory (echoing Richard Hoggart and Matthew Arnold), Assertion (A) argues that arts criticize life obliquely through imaginative form, and Reason (R) directly explains why this oblique aesthetic operation fulfills a vital, indispensable social function.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of derivational morpheme ?
items.explanation: Derivational morphemes create new words or alter lexical categories. While '-ship' forms an abstract noun, in the UGC answer key option (1) friend – friendship was designated, distinguishing it from adjectival and participial category-shifting derivations.

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II
items.stem: Which of these statements is incorrect about presentism and its basic premises ?
options: ugh Grady is its principal proponent.
Our knowledge of works from the past is conditioned by and dependent upon the ideologies of the present.
Presentism does not contextualize cultural production in the same way or make use of the theorists that New istoricism does.
istoricism itself necessarily produces an implicit allegory of the present in its configuration of the past.
items.explanation: Presentism in Shakespeare and early modern studies (championed by Hugh Grady, Terence Hawkes, and Evelyn Gajowski) deliberately engages contemporary theory and historical context, so the statement that it does not contextualize cultural production or use theory is incorrect.

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson, John Milton
items.stem:
“Where there is leisure for fiction, there is little grief”, was Samuel Johnson’s criticism of a
famous poem. Which poem was it ?
options: Thomas Gray’s “Elegy Written on a Country Churchyard”
items.explanation: In his Life of Milton in Lives of the English Poets (1779), Dr. Samuel Johnson famously attacked John Milton's pastoral elegy 'Lycidas', writing: 'Where there is leisure for fiction, there is little grief... Its form is that of a pastoral, easy, vulgar, and therefore disgusting.'

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Thomas Mann
items.stem:
The story is rounded in the forbidden nature of Aschenbach’s Obsession with a young
boy; its author ultimately links the obsession with death, disease and esthetic disintegration.
The author of the story is :
items.explanation: Thomas Mann's novella Death in Venice (Der Tod in Venedig, 1912) depicts the aging Munich writer Gustav von Aschenbach, whose repressed, aestheticized infatuation with the Polish youth Tadzio leads to his physical and moral disintegration amid a cholera epidemic.

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Which of the following novels of Joseph Conrad is set in Malay ?
items.explanation: Joseph Conrad's Lord Jim (1900) follows the disgraced British seaman Jim after the Patna abandonment scandal into the remote, jungle interior of Patusan in the Malay Archipelago, where he attempts to redeem his honor among the Bugis community.

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Nuruddin Farah
items.stem: Nuruddin Farah’s Maps tells the story of __________.
items.explanation: Somali novelist Nuruddin Farah's acclaimed novel Maps (1986), the first volume of his Blood in the Sun trilogy, focuses on the orphaned youth Askar growing up during the 1977 Ogaden War between Somalia and Ethiopia, exploring national and personal identity.

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Keats
items.stem:
One of the most quoted statements on poetry by John Keats is reproduced with blanks
below. Complete the statement with correct words.
“If Poetry __________ as naturally as the leaves to a tree, it __________ at all”.
options: does not come; had better not come
come not; had better not come
items.explanation: In a letter to his publisher John Taylor on 27 February 1818, John Keats articulated his 'axioms' of poetics, including: 'That if Poetry come not as naturally as the Leaves to a tree it had better not come at all.'

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Manohar Malgonkar
items.stem:
Manohar Malgonkar was a hunter, a lieutenant colonel in the British army, and a tea-planter.
e also wrote a memorable novel about the Sepoy Mutiny, especially Peshwa Baji Rao II.
What is that novel ?
items.explanation: Manohar Malgonkar's historical novel The Devil's Wind (1972) reconstructs the 1857 Indian Uprising from the viewpoint of Nana Saheb, the adopted heir of Peshwa Baji Rao II, presenting a sympathetic Indian historical revision of the events at Kanpur.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter, John Fowles
items.stem:
Who wrote the screenplay for the film version of John Fowles’s novel The French Lieutenant’s
Woman ?
items.explanation: British dramatist Harold Pinter wrote the acclaimed, Oscar-nominated screenplay for Karel Reisz's 1981 film adaptation of John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman, innovatively structuring it as a film-within-a-film featuring actors playing the Victorian lovers.

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
“ow all their plays be neither right tragedies, nor right comedies, mingling kings and clowns,
not because the matter so carrieth it, but thrust in the clown by head and shoulders to play a
part in majestical matters”.
What term does Philip Sidney use to characterize such plays and which of the unities of
Aristotle do they violate ?
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (1595), Sir Philip Sidney condemns Renaissance playwrights who produce 'mongrel tragicomedy' by indiscriminately mixing kings and clowns, thereby violating the classical Aristotelian unity of action.

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
There is a large number of religious poems in Old English Poetry. One of the finest is the
Dream of the Rood. The words ‘the Rood’ in the title means :
items.explanation: The Dream of the Rood is an Old English religious dream-vision poem preserved in the 10th-century Vercelli Book, in which the True Cross (Old English 'rōd', meaning rod, pole, or cross) is personified and speaks of Christ's crucifixion as a heroic triumph.

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · M. Anantanarayanan
items.stem:
Identify from among the following, the one incorrect statement on M. Anantanarayanan’s
Silver Pilgrimage (1961) :
options: M. Anantanarayanan modelled this narrative on the well-known picaresque novels in English.
The Silver Pilgrimage is M. Anantanarayanan’s only foray into fiction.
This novel is mainly an account of the adventures of Jayasurya, a Sri Lankan prince of the sixteenth century.
Among the literary texts quoted by the novel are lines from Shakespeare, Donne and Rilke and classical Tamil poets.
items.explanation: M. Anantanarayanan's The Silver Pilgrimage (1961) is structured on ancient Indian Sanskrit and Tamil puranic/katha narrative traditions rather than English picaresque models, making statement (1) incorrect.

items.title: Q40 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Frank Kermode, Northrop Frye
items.stem:
Listed below are the titles of some influential books by Frank Kermode. Identify which one
of the titles that does NOT belong to the set.
options: The Great Code : The Bible and Literature
items.explanation: The Great Code: The Bible and Literature (1982) was written by Canadian myth and archetype critic Northrop Frye, whereas The Sense of an Ending (1967), The Genesis of Secrecy (1979), and the memoir Not Entitled (1995) are major works by Frank Kermode.

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden, Joseph Addison
items.stem: Identify the one erroneous statement on Neoclassicism listed below :
options: Lodovico Castelvetro and Torquato Tasso reatly influenced English writers like Milton and Dryden.
Neoclassicism took its final form during the reign of Louis XIV (1638-1715).
Boilean’s L’Art poétique influenced Pope’s Essay on Criticism.
The English relation to Neoclassicism was one of dialogue. Most literally, this dialogue is effected in Addison’s An Essay on Dramatic Poesy.
items.explanation: Statement (4) is erroneous because An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668) was written by John Dryden, not Joseph Addison; Addison was an Augustan essayist associated with The Tatler and The Spectator.

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · A. K. Ramanujan
items.stem:
In his Poems of Love and War, a collection of classic Indian poems in English translation,
A.K. Ramanujan sought to revive an ancient __________ poetic tradition. Choose the right
word.
items.explanation: In Poems of Love and War (1985), A. K. Ramanujan masterfully translated classic Tamil Sangam poetry from the Eight Anthologies (Ettuttokai), reviving the ancient Akam (interior/love) and Puram (exterior/war) poetic conventions for Anglophone readers.

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: American Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.stem:
Arrange the following sentences in the order in which they appear in Emerson’s
“Self-Reliance” :
(a)
To be great is to be misunderstood.
(b)
Pythagoras was misunderstood, and Socrates, and Jesus, and Luther, and Copernicus,
and Galileo, and Newton, and every pure and wise spirit that ever took flesh.
(c)
If it so bad then to be misunderstood!
(d)
It is a right fool’s word.
(e)
Misunderstood!
items.explanation: In Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 'Self-Reliance' (1841), the memorable passage reads: 'Misunderstood! (e) It is a right fool’s word. (d) Is it so bad then to be misunderstood? (c) Pythagoras was misunderstood, and Socrates... (b) To be great is to be misunderstood. (a)'

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit I: Drama · Oscar Wilde
items.stem:
X ... Do you know it is nearly seven ?
Y (irritably) Oh! it always is nearly seven.
X well, I’m hungry.
Y I never knew you when you weren’t ...
X What shall we do after dinner ? Go to a theatre ?
Y Oh no! I loathe listening.
X Well, let us o to the club ?
Y Oh no! I hate talking.
X Well, we might trot round to the Empire at ten ?
Y Oh no! I can’t bear looking at things.
It is so silly.
X Well, what shall we do ?
Y Nothing!
X It is awfully hard work doing nothing. owever, I don’t mind hard work where there is no
definite object of any kind.
Identify the speakers in this dialogue :
options: Algernon (X) to Jack (Y) The Importance of Being Earnest
Lucky (X) to Pozzo (Y) Waiting for Godot
Man (X) to the Woman (Y) The Waste Land
items.explanation: This witty, languid exchange between the dandy Algernon Moncrieff (X) and Jack Worthing (Y) occurs in Act I of Oscar Wilde's masterpiece of high Victorian comedy, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895).

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare, Euripides
items.stem: Which of these Greek plays was a source for The Winter’s Tale ?
items.explanation: Shakespeare's romance The Winter's Tale (1611) draws directly upon Euripides' tragicomedy Alcestis, where Queen Alcestis dies for her husband Admetus and is brought back from the underworld veiled by Heracles, paralleling the miraculous restoration of Hermione.

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem:
Sweet is the lore which nature brings;
Our meddling intellect
Mis-shapes the beauteous forms of things :
We murder to dissect.
– Wordsworth
Which of the following best summarises the speaker’s position ?
options: Nature is incomplete without a human witness to attest to its beauty.
uman endeavours will succeed only if the laws of nature are taken into account.
Nature yields a pleasure superior to that derived from intrusive human inquiry
The flaws inherent in human nature are also evident in the natural world.
items.explanation: In 'The Tables Turned' (Lyrical Ballads, 1798), William Wordsworth urges his friend to leave books and science behind, cautioning that intellectual dissection destroys organic beauty: 'Sweet is the lore which nature brings; / Our meddling intellect / Mis-shapes the beauteous forms of things: / We murder to dissect.'

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II · Jean Baudrillard
items.stem:
(a)
Jean Baudrillard tells us that postmodern societies are marked by simulacra.
(b)
By simulacra he means non-representations of reality.
(c)
Simulacra artificially produce a mediated world masquerading as authenticity.
(d)
It was not Jean Baudrillard but his interpreters who coined the term “simulacra”.
Which of the above statements are true ?
items.explanation: In Simulacra and Simulation (1981), French cultural theorist Jean Baudrillard argues that postmodernity is marked by simulacra (a), which artificially manufacture a hyperreal world that masks the total absence of profound reality (c); statements (a) and (c) are true.

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following is correct as the natural order of language acquisition ?
items.explanation: In language pedagogy and applied linguistics, the natural sequence of language skills acquisition is represented by the universal acronym LSRW: Listening first, followed by Speaking, Reading, and ultimately Writing.

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit II: Poetry · Derek Walcott
items.stem: Which of the following statements is NOT TRUE regarding the poems of Derek Walcott ?
options: is poem “Goats and Monkeys” has an epigraph from Shakespeare’s Othello
In “The Sadhu of Couva” Walcott refers to Diwali, anuman and the Ramayana
Walcott has written a poem entitled “Jean Rhys”
In “A Far Cry From Africa” Walcott depicts his divided loyalties in the context of the Changuna Uprising
items.explanation: Derek Walcott's famous poem 'A Far Cry from Africa' (In a Green Night, 1962) explores his divided Caribbean-British-African identity against the historical backdrop of the Mau Mau Uprising in 1950s Kenya, NOT the fictional 'Changuna Uprising'.

items.title: Q50 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Renaissance & Elizabethan · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare’s time who owned the rights to a theatrical script ?
options: the patron of the acting company
items.explanation: In Elizabethan and Jacobean England, playwrights sold their play scripts outright to the joint-stock theatrical playing companies (such as the Lord Chamberlain's Men), which then owned exclusive performance rights and promptbooks.

items.title: Q51 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following sentences uses more than three cohesive devices ?
options: At that time a person could drive for miles without seeing a house.
All of them could recite the poem yesterday.
You can use a pencil, though not a pen, to write your name.
As soon as Mohan entered the stadium the crowd cheered.
items.explanation: In M. A. K. Halliday and Ruqaiya Hasan's cohesion theory, the sentence 'You can use a pencil, though not a pen, to write your name' incorporates multiple cohesive devices: adversative conjunction ('though'), ellipsis of predicate ('[you can] not [use] a pen'), and lexical substitution/contrast.

items.title: Q52 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit VI: English in India · William Jones, Nathaniel Halhed
items.stem:
Match the columns :
Indian Text
English Translator
(a)
The love of Kamarupa and Kamalata
(i)
William Jones

items.title: Q53 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which of the following is NOT TRUE of the New Bolt Report, “The Teaching of English in
England” ?
options: It urged the teaching of the national literature.
It proposed the teaching of English Literature at the university level.
It aimed at uniting divided classes after the war.
items.explanation: The Newbolt Report (The Teaching of English in England, 1921), chaired by Sir Henry Newbolt, aimed to unify British social classes through elementary and secondary school literature education rather than emphasizing elite university curricula.

items.title: Q54 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Middleton
items.stem:
This revenge tragedy opens with the long soliloquy of the protagonist carrying the skull of
his poisoned fianceand swearing vengeance for the old Duke who has committed the
vicious act. Identify the play.
items.explanation: Thomas Middleton's Jacobean revenge tragedy The Revenger's Tragedy (1607) opens famously with the malcontent Vindice holding the skull of his poisoned fiancée Gloriana in his hands, swearing bloody retribution against the corrupt old Duke.

items.title: Q55 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Anthony Trollope
items.stem: What did Anthony Trollope seek to criticize through the character Mr. Slope ?
items.explanation: In Anthony Trollope's Barchester Towers (1857), the oily, ambitious domestic chaplain Mr. Obadiah Slope is drawn as a caustic satire of hypocritical, narrow-minded evangelical 'Low Church' clergy infringing upon the traditional cathedral establishment.

items.title: Q56 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Literary Theory & Cultural Studies · Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II
items.stem:
“To refer to symbols as ‘Lacanian symbols’, to dub self-doubt as ‘Lacanian self-doubt’, and to
call reflections in a mirror ‘Lacanian reflections’ is not to read the mind from a perspective
informed by Lacan. Nor do parenthetical references to Barthes’ hermeneutic code and
Foucault’s analysis of sexual discourse constitute an interpretation necessarily different from
that of traditional humanist criticism”.
The author of the passage is objecting to critics who __________.
options: try to force a parallel between recent critical approaches and traditional humanist criticism.
decoratively apply the names and terminology of recent critical theories without employing the methodology.
attempt to reduce the study of literature to a hunt for coded messages and symbols.
stubbornly maintain a traditional notion of the role of criticism while refusing to acknowledge new theoretical developments.
items.explanation: The quoted passage objects to academic critics who mechanically and decoratively sprinkle poststructuralist terminology ('Lacanian', 'hermeneutic code', 'Foucault') into their writing without genuinely adopting the radical epistemological methodologies of those thinkers.

items.title: Q57 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Peter Ackroyd, Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Peter Ackroyd’s first novel, The Great Fire of London, picks up the historical echoes and
artfully deploys a Dickens novel as an intertext. Identify the source Dickens text.
items.explanation: Peter Ackroyd's debut novel The Great Fire of London (1982) artfully weaves Charles Dickens's Little Dorrit into its contemporary storyline, following filmmakers and eccentric Londoners obsessed with filming an adaptation inside the vanished Marshalsea debtor's prison.

items.title: Q58 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit I: Drama · Henrik Ibsen
items.stem:
Which of the following plays by enrik Ibsen deals with the perils that await the
emancipated woman in a society which is not ready to accept her ?
items.explanation: Henrik Ibsen's Hedda Gabler (1890) portrays the aristocratic, intellectually fierce Hedda, trapped in a stultifying bourgeois marriage to Jörgen Tesman and hemmed in by provincial Victorian decorum, whose frustrated refusal to submit leads to her tragic suicide.

items.title: Q59 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Virginia Woolf
items.stem:
“Yet it is the masculine values that prevail”, observed a famous writer “Speaking cruelly”,
she continued, “football and sport are ‘important’, the worship of fashion, the buying of
clothes ‘trivial’.”
Name the author and the text.
options: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own
Jean Rhys, After Leaving Mr. Mackenzie
items.explanation: In Chapter 4 of A Room of One's Own (1929), Virginia Woolf observes the pervasive gendered hierarchy of cultural valuation: 'Speaking cruelly, football and sport are "important"; the worship of fashion, the buying of clothes "trivial". And these values are inevitably transferred from life to fiction.'

items.title: Q60 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem:
According to coleridge, the “secondary imagination” “dissolves, diffuses, __________, in
order to recreate...”.
Choose the right word for the blank.
items.explanation: In Chapter XIII of Biographia Literaria (1817), Samuel Taylor Coleridge famously defines the secondary imagination as an echo of the primary: 'It dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to recreate; or where this process is rendered impossible, yet still at all events it struggles to idealize and to unify.'

items.title: Q61 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Beginning 1996, an Indian publisher commenced the publication of a series of modern
Indian novels in English translation. By 2003, it had published eighty novels of repute from
almost all Indian languages. Identify the publisher.
items.explanation: Beginning in 1996, Macmillan India launched the major project 'Modern Indian Novels in Translation' (curated by translation editor Mini Krishnan), publishing over eighty canonical regional Indian novels translated into English across several years.

items.title: Q62 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Old & Middle English · Unit II: Poetry · William Dunbar
items.stem: William Dunbar’s Lament for the makers is about :
items.explanation: Middle Scots poet William Dunbar composed the elegiac 'Lament for the Makaris' ('makaris' being the Scots term for poets or makers) around 1505, repeating the solemn liturgical refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' as he mourns Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Henryson, and others.

items.title: Q63 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Victorian Age · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Who among the following protagonists of Thomas ardy feels his lot as akin to Job’s ?
items.explanation: In Thomas Hardy's Jude the Obscure (1895), following the murder of his children by Little Father Time and his abandonment by Sue Bridehead, the broken Jude Fawley lies dying on Remembrance Day in Christminster bitterly reciting Job 3 ('Let the day perish wherein I was born').

items.title: Q64 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit II: Poetry · Kamau Brathwaite
items.stem: Edward Brathwaite’s poem “Calypso” assumes that you are familiar with __________.
options: the business of Calypso during the Middle Passage
the West Indian music in syncopated African rhythm
the folk ways and mores of Trinidadian merchants
items.explanation: Barbadian poet Kamau Brathwaite's poem 'Calypso' (from The Arrivants) uses syncopated polyrhythms, steel-pan cadences, and Creole speech patterns rooted in the Afro-Caribbean musical tradition of Trinidadian calypso.

items.title: Q65 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-War British, Movement & Postmodernism · Unit I: Drama · Edward Bond, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Which of the modern plays by a British playwright actually puts Shakespeare as character
on stage ?
items.explanation: Edward Bond's politically provocative play Bingo: Scenes of Money and Death (1973) dramatizes William Shakespeare in retirement at New Place in Stratford-upon-Avon, examining the tragic moral contradiction between his poetic genius and his complicity as a propertied landlord.

items.title: Q66 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Edmund Burke
items.stem:
A famous challenge to the Neoclassical tenets of form and reason in aesthetic considerations
came from Edmund Burke. is work was titled :
options: An Enquiry into the Philosophical Origin of, Our Ideas of the sublime and the Beautiful
Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and the Beautiful
An Enquiry into the Philosophical Origin of Our Ideas of the Beautiful and the Sublime
Philosophical Enquiry into Our Original Ideas of the Beautiful and the Sublime
items.explanation: Edmund Burke published A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful in 1757, challenging Neoclassical rationalism by rooting aesthetic response to the sublime in terror, obscurity, infinity, and physiological emotion.

items.title: Q67 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: English Language & Linguistics · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Match the following :
List-A
List-B
(a)
The Grammar - Translation Method
(i)
comprehensible input
(b)
The Direct Method
(ii)
strategic use of mother tongue
(c)
Total Physical Response
(iii)
shuns mother tongue
(d)
The Natural Approach
(iv)
oral input
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: In ELT methodology: Grammar-Translation employs strategic translation into the mother tongue (ii); Direct Method strictly shuns the mother tongue (iii); Total Physical Response uses imperative oral commands requiring physical action (iv); and the Natural Approach relies on comprehensible input (i).

items.title: Q68 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction, short story · Amitav Ghosh
items.stem:
Which of these works by Indian writers does NOT have the Naxalite Movement as a
background ?
items.explanation: Amitav Ghosh's The Shadow Lines (1988) examines the 1947 Partition of Bengal, the 1964 communal riots in Dhaka and Calcutta, and the London Blitz; unlike Mahasweta Devi's Mother of 1084, Neel Mukherjee's The Lives of Others, and Jhumpa Lahiri's The Lowland, it does NOT feature the Naxalite movement.

items.title: Q69 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit II: Poetry · John Dryden
items.stem:
“So when the last and dreadful hour
This crumbling pageant shall devour,
The trumpet shall be heard on high,
The dead shall live, the living die,
And music shall untune the sky”
These are the closing lines of a famous poem.
Identify the poem.
items.explanation: John Dryden's celebrated ode 'A Song for St. Cecilia's Day' (1687) concludes with the magnificent Grand Chorus envisioning the Day of Judgment: 'The trumpet shall be heard on high, / The dead shall live, the living die, / And music shall untune the sky.'

items.title: Q70 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Augustan / Neo-Classical Age · Unit II: Poetry · James Thomson
items.stem:
This eighteenth-century English poem imitates spenser in stanza form and in allegorical
narrative H: passers H- by are lured by an enchanter with promises of ease, luxury, and
aesthetic delight, then consigned to a dungeon where they languish in apathy and
impotence until the Knight of Arts and Industry dissolves the spell. Identify the poem.
items.explanation: James Thomson's allegorical poem The Castle of Indolence (1748) is composed in Spenserian stanzas, depicting pilgrims seduced into apathy and sensory languor by the wizard Indolence until they are liberated by the Knight of Arts and Industry.

items.title: Q71 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Virginia Woolf, Leonard Woolf
items.stem: Which of the following statements on the ogarth press is FALSE ?
options: The ogarth press was founded in 1917 by Leonard and Virginia Woolf
Its location was their home, called ogarth ouse
The press was solely devoted to publishing international classics in translation
The press published translations of Gorky, Chekhov, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Rilke, Svevo and others
items.explanation: The Hogarth Press, established by Leonard and Virginia Woolf at Hogarth House in Richmond in 1917, was an eclectic modernist press that championed experimental original British writing (including Woolf's own novels and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land), not solely translated works.

items.title: Q72 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Jamaica Kincaid
items.stem:
Read the below passage and answer questions 72 to 75 that follow :

THE ANTIGUA THAT I knew, the Antigua in which I grew up, is not the Antigua you, a tourist, would see now. That Antigua no longer exists. That Antigua no longer exists partly for the usual reason, the passing of time, and partly because the bad-minded people who used to rule over it, the English, no longer do so. (But the English have become such a pitiful lot these days, with hardly any idea what to do with themselves now that they no longer have one quarter of the earth's human population bowing and scraping before them. They don't seem to know that this empire business was all wrong and they should, at least, be wearing sackcloth and ashes in token penance of the wrongs committed, the irrevocableness of their bad deeds, for no natural disaster imaginable could equal the harm they did. Actual death might have been better. And so all this fuss over empire – what went wrong here, what went wrong there – always makes me quite crazy, for I can say to them what went wrong : they should never have left their home, their precious England, a place they loved so much, a place they had to leave but could never forget. And so everywhere they went they turned it into England; and everybody they met they turned English. But no place could ever really be England, and nobody who did not look exactly like them would ever be English, so you can imagine the destruction of people and land that came from that. The English hate each other and they hate England, and the reason they are so miserable now is that they have no place else to go and nobody else to feel better than.)

To whom is the passage directly addressed ?
items.explanation: In A Small Place (1988), Jamaica Kincaid employs an intensely confrontational second-person address ('you, a tourist... an ugly, empty thing, a stupid thing') directly indicting North American and European tourists enjoying their tropical holiday oblivious to colonial scars.

items.title: Q73 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Jamaica Kincaid

The English hate each other and they hate England, and the reason they are so miserable now is that they have no place else to go and nobody else to feel better than.)

The English feel extremely miserable because :
options: They do not have anyone else to feel superior to
They have been reduced to a state of non-entity
They have no lands to colonise
items.explanation: In her scathing analysis, Kincaid writes that the post-imperial English are pitiful and miserable because, having lost an empire where a quarter of the world bowed before them, 'they have no place else to go and nobody else to feel better than.'

items.title: Q74 · Dec 2015 (Paper III)
items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Jamaica Kincaid

Do the British realize that colonizing countries was a bad practice, according to the
narrator ?
options: The narrator is rather unsure they do
The narrator is rather unsure they don’t
items.explanation: The narrator states that the English 'don’t seem to know that this empire business was all wrong', observing with sharp irony that they fail to show the sackcloth-and-ashes penance that would demonstrate moral comprehension of the catastrophic harm done.

items.meta: Postcolonial & World Literatures · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Jamaica Kincaid

Which of the following best describes the content of the extract ?
options: The speaker fervently desires better understanding between the English and the colonized people in post colonial times
The speaker is interested in nostalgic tours of emigre antiguans to their childhood home
The speaker whose childhood was spent in Antigua reports the great change currently evident in the pungent irony
The speaker is making a case for the penance of the English, the erstwhile rulers of Antigua.
items.explanation: The extract from A Small Place features an autobiographical Antiguan narrator who revisits her childhood island, measuring the irreversible historical and physical transformations through pungent, biting anti-colonial irony directed at both colonizers and tourists.
